summary: This informational document specifies generic requirements for a protocol that lets Path Computation Clients ask Path Computation Elements for paths, and lets PCEs cooperate with each other. Later documents give application-specific requirements for the PCE communication protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4657 lists what a communication protocol must support when a network component asks another component to calculate a path. It covers the request and reply, along with security, scale, and recovery needs, but defines no protocol itself.

questions: what is a path computation element
what are pce communication protocol requirements
what constraints can a pce request include
subtitle: A requirements checklist for communication between path-computation clients and elements.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Client needs a way to request a path from a remote Path Computation Element, and PCEs may also need to cooperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for requests, responses, constraints, reliability, security, scaling, liveness detection, policies, and recovery.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol. Application-specific requirements are left to separate documents.

today: RFC 4657 is an Informational document published in September 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it states generic requirements and leaves application-specific requirements to other documents.

sections.title: The PCE Communication Model
sections.content:
A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) to calculate a network path. The request includes a source and destination, and may include constraints or an objective function. The PCE uses a network graph based on its Traffic Engineering Database.

A remote PCC and PCE need a request-response protocol. PCEs may also request paths from other PCEs, so the RFC assumes one protocol can serve both kinds of communication. A co-located PCC and PCE do not require a communication protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCC asks a PCE for a path between two points. The request can include rules, and the PCE returns a path or explains that it could not calculate one.

sections.title: Requests, Responses, and Notifications
sections.content:
A request must identify its endpoints and support constraints, such as bandwidth, included or excluded resources, and path disjointness. The requester must be able to choose supported objective functions, such as a shortest path or a least-loaded path. A response returns explicit paths and may include path costs or bandwidth; an unsuccessful computation receives a negative response.

The protocol must allow cancellation, multiple requests and paths in a message, and correlated continuation messages when results span messages. Communication is asynchronous: a PCC can send another request without waiting for the first reply, and responses identify their requests. Notifications may also be sent without a request.
sections.plainLanguage: A request says where the path starts and ends, plus any limits the requester needs. A reply gives a path or a failure, and each reply identifies the request it answers.

sections.title: Constraints and Path Objectives
sections.content:
The generic constraints include bandwidth, affinity, link, node, and Shared Risk Link Group inclusion or exclusion; maximum IGP or traffic-engineering metrics; hop count; and path disjointness. MPLS traffic engineering adds class type and protection constraints. GMPLS adds switching, encoding, and link-protection types.

Supported unsynchronized objectives include minimum cost for a chosen metric, least-loaded path, and maximum available bandwidth. Supported synchronized objectives include reducing total bandwidth use, increasing residual bandwidth on the most-loaded link, and reducing total cost across diverse paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Constraints describe what a path must or must not use. An objective tells the PCE what to prefer when several paths meet those rules.

sections.title: Reliability, Scale, and Recovery
sections.content:
The protocol must support reliable delivery, detect lost or damaged messages, retransmit when needed, handle duplicates and ordering, provide flow control, and detect communication failures quickly. It should use an existing transport with congestion control and must not impose a message-size limit. It must indicate congestion and rate-limiting state.

The RFC gives scale targets of 1000 PCCs and 100 PCEs per domain, 20 domains, an average of 10 request messages per second per PCE, and bursts of 100 per second per PCE within a 10-second interval. After failure, the protocol must support liveness checks and resynchronize requests and information. Restoration and re-optimization requests can include the prior path.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol must keep working during request bursts and recover its shared information after a connection failure. It must also tell each side whether the other side or the network connection has failed.

sections.title: Security, Policy, and Management
sections.content:
The protocol must protect requests and responses against impersonation, interception, and denial of service. It must provide key management for message authenticity and integrity. A PCE may have local policy against returning explicit paths; in that case it must return an error when a client requests one.

The protocol must support accepting or rejecting requests under policy, detect liveness, and recover after communication failure. Operators need separate management information for PCCs and PCEs, statistics on malformed or unauthorized messages and congestion drops, notifications, and diagnostic tools.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized clients should be able to ask for paths, and clients need a way to verify the PCE's replies. Operators also need tools to see failures, congestion, and request results.
